prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock, based on magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms, and its development to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I keep B006 as my preferred prize after the full first-round exchange. The chair asks what the lattice clock adds beyond the 2005 and 2012 prizes in wording that does not claim the comb or the ion-clock lineages, and I think the answer can be stated precisely. The 2005 citation covers precision laser spectroscopy and the frequency comb, which is the counting tool; the 2012 citation covers control and measurement of individual quantum systems, whose clock embodiment is the single trapped ion. Katori's idea is different in kind: choosing a wavelength at which the ground and excited clock states see the same light shift removes the trade-off between trapping and perturbation, so thousands of neutral atoms are interrogated at once without Doppler or recoil shifts. That is what makes the improved statistics and the 10^-18 regime reachable, and it is the architecture now reproduced in several national laboratories. The citation I propose names the lattice concept and the development to 10^-18, and names neither the comb nor ion control. The other points in favour are unchanged: the two-name credit maps onto concept and realisation to extreme accuracy, interpretation is stable because the results are reproduced and compared across laboratories, and consequences are already physical, including millimetre-scale redshift, bounds on varying constants and the pending redefinition of the second. On Pearce's point that the redefinition is a reason to wait, I would say the prize rewards the discovery and its demonstrated performance, not the ceremony that follows from it.
statement.case_against: I take the continuity objection as the strongest one, and I note that it is now the main objection raised by Mehlig, Pearce, Eriksson and, with less weight, Johansson and Danielsson. If the committee reads the lattice clock as a very large improvement in precision inside a field already honoured twice, the case weakens, and that is a judgement about novelty that no one can settle with evidence. Credit boundaries also remain: ion-clock groups and other lattice-clock laboratories at NIST, PTB, SYRTE and Tokyo have claims that a two-name citation does not acknowledge, and Johansson is right that Ye's place relative to the comb lineage deserves an explicit check. B004 is conceptually deeper and has the broadest opening support, and I accept that a committee which puts new organising principles above measurement achievement can defensibly choose it. My own difficulty with B004 is attribution: Molenkamp's experiment tested the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, Zhang is deceased, and a trio that omits that step is tidier than the history. Even a narrow quantum spin Hall citation leaves that gap visible, though I agree with Johansson that it does not disqualify the award.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B006 eighth because he reads the lattice clock as a precision refinement of the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and holds B009 first while accepting that B004 is safer on maturity.
responses.response: I still disagree on incrementalism, and the chair's question is the right test. A refinement improves the number that an existing architecture produces. Magic-wavelength trapping changed the architecture, because it removed the conflict between holding many atoms and keeping them unperturbed. That is a concept and not a better laser lock. I also grant that B009 has a rare prediction-then-discovery structure and that waiting for a mechanism could be open-ended. But the discovery is not the debated part, and what troubles me is on the experimental side: the credit rests on Jarillo-Herrero alone, with Cao and the parallel groups outside the set, whereas the clock credit does not have that hole. Your statement that the Z2 classification extends the programme recognised in 2016 is a fair point, and I take it as a reason that B004 should not be treated as an automatic default.

responses.point: Pearce calls B006 largely a precision advance in a field honoured in 2005 and says the pending redefinition of the second is a reason to wait, not to prefer B006 now, while naming it his first alternative.
responses.response: I agree that a prize should not be justified by an event that has not happened, and I do not rest on the redefinition. I rest on the demonstrated 10^-18 performance, its reproduction in several laboratories, and results such as the millimetre redshift measurement that have already been obtained. On the 2005 overlap, I separate the counting tool from the thing counted: the comb made optical clocks usable, but the lattice with a magic wavelength is what made a many-atom optical clock accurate. I also agree with your request that the credit gap for B004 be stated openly in the record. I would ask that the equally real credit boundary for B006, namely the ion-clock and other lattice groups, be recorded with the same openness.

responses.point: Johansson prefers B004 with a citation narrowed to the quantum spin Hall effect and its first observation, agrees B006 has the cleanest allocation, and asks for a separate check of Ye's credit relative to the comb lineage and of my Hall-laboratory connection.
responses.response: The check is reasonable and I welcome it. On the record, Ye's contribution here is carrying Katori's lattice concept to the 10^-18 regime, including the strontium systematics and the redshift measurements, and that is distinct from the comb work for which Hall and Hansch were recognised, even though the comb is used in the clock. I would write the citation around the lattice concept so that Ye's credit does not depend on the comb at all. I also accept your narrow-citation approach for B004: if the committee prefers that prize, limiting it to the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect and its first observation is the right way to keep the three-dimensional work and the credit gap from spreading. I do not move to B004 on that basis, because the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap is within the quantum spin Hall effect itself, not in the three-dimensional work.

responses.point: Olsson treats lineage continuity as the main objection the committee must answer, wants the citation to state the invention explicitly, and discloses a Tokyo and JSPS link while moving from B012 to B006.
responses.response: I agree with how you frame it. Treating continuity as an objection to be answered, not as a strength, is more honest, and my proposed wording states the invention of the optical lattice clock with magic-wavelength trapping explicitly, so that the answer sits in the citation. I am glad to have a second supporter who reached B006 after changing her ranking, and I want the committee to see that my support did not depend on her. On disclosures, I think yours and mine are of the same kind, an institutional or training-period connection with no documented collaboration, and the committee should treat them alike.

responses.point: Eriksson would be comfortable with B006 as a prize but weighs conceptual reach more, holds that the Hall, Hansch and Wineland prizes narrow its novelty, and keeps it as an alternative.
responses.response: We agree on the facts and differ on weights, which is what the committee should debate. I would accept that B004 changed how a community thinks about electronic phases. But conceptual reach is not the only criterion for a discovery prize; a measurement capability that opens a regime in which new physics can be tested, and that is already demonstrated, is also a discovery. On the narrowing by earlier prizes, I think the opposite follows from what those prizes honoured: the comb and the ion were the enabling methods, and neither delivered the lattice architecture or a 10^-18 clock with many atoms. I also see a difference in the credit: your own view is that the B004 credit gap is a real reservation, and for B006 the names are a clean pair.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the lattice clock as a new architecture or as a precision step within the 2005 and 2012 lineage; this is a judgement about novelty that evidence does not settle.
Whether ion-clock groups or other lattice-clock laboratories have a claim that makes the Katori-Ye pair look incomplete, and how Ye's credit should be separated from the comb.
Whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission for B004 is accepted by the committee, which would remove my main reason for placing B006 ahead of it.
I recall dates and uncertainty figures from memory and have not verified them against the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. My profile documents a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my doctoral period, and Jun Ye's career emerged from that milieu. I have no documented collaboration, supervision or institutional tie with Katori or Ye. Lindroth does not think recusal is needed on that basis alone and Johansson would minute the connection and check Ye's credit separately; I agree with that approach and will accept the committee's decision on whether I should step back from B006. I also record that my Lund work on laser stabilisation, rare-earth quantum memories and optical coherence is adjacent to precision laser metrology, but I have no specific conflict from it.
